prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a case where one idea (the magic wavelength, which cancels the lattice light shift) was followed by decisive experiments and by years of systematic work that any experimentalist can check. Katori proposed and demonstrated the concept, and Ye's group took it to the 10^-18 level and added many-body physics (spin-exchange and correlated clocks) and gravitational-redshift measurements across a millimetre-scale sample. The result has been reproduced and compared across JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL and others, with Sr, Yb and Hg, so it is robust in the sense I care about. It makes a basic quantum phenomenon visible and controllable: a many-atom quantum system with essentially no perturbation of the clock transition. The credit is a clean two-person split that the whole committee proposed independently. This is the only candidate that all eight of us ranked, which carries weight even though opening support is not the same as scientific merit. I move it from fifth on my own opening ballot to my preferred configuration for two reasons: the arguments of Kroll and Lindroth, and my own reading of the overlap and conflict problems around my former first choice.
statement.case_against: Whether this is a new regime of physics or an extraordinary refinement of a measurement is a fair question, and the SI second has not yet been redefined, so one could argue we should wait. The frequency-comb prize of 2005 and the ion-control prize of 2012 are close neighbours, and Lemonde, Takamoto and the ion-clock groups (Wineland, Rosenband, Schmidt) have real claims that a two-name prize leaves out. Against my former first choice, B039, the main problem is that the 2025 prize to Clarke, Devoret and Martinis already recognised the superconducting-circuit platform, and circuit QED would look like a second prize for the same chip family only a year later. Girvin and Huang are also outside the supplied credit, so the theory share is unresolved. Against the clocks the strongest point is that the discovery element is smaller than the instrument element. I accept that this is a close judgement.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks turned the magic-wavelength idea into the most precise measurement instruments ever built, with independent confirmation by many groups and a clean Katori and Ye credit, supporting timely recognition while the second redefinition is under discussion.
responses.response: I agree on the experimental side and on the attribution. I would add one qualification: the argument for recognising it now should rest on the physics (a controlled many-atom quantum system, many-body effects, tests of gravitational redshift at sub-millimetre scales), not on the SI-redefinition timetable, because that is a metrological decision the committee should not follow. I also read your B009 and B039 rankings as closer to mine than your opening ranks suggest, and I would be happy to see trapped ions come later; I disagree only that the Wineland prize is a minor concern there.

responses.point: Circuit QED is the working basis of superconducting processors but sits partly in engineering and close to the 2025 prize topic, so recognition so soon could be seen as premature or redundant. She ranks the lattice clocks first, calling it precision atomic physics at its best.
responses.response: Your reservation about circuit QED is the one that moved me, and it is stronger coming from outside my own field. I put B039 first because strong coupling of one photon to one artificial atom on a chip is a new regime that the 2025 prize did not cover, but I cannot claim that a committee would see that separation as clean one year later. I also disagree gently with your description of the transmon as a reason for the Yale credit: the transmon was the Yale theory and experiment work (Koch et al.), not the proposal I am arguing for, so it should not enter the attribution here.

responses.point: Topological insulators have a clear theory-plus-two-experiments structure (Kane, Molenkamp, Xue), and she ranks it first with strong maturity; she is more hesitant about whether two individuals fairly represent the IceCube collaboration.
responses.response: I agree with your concerns about IceCube attribution and share them, which is one reason B014 sits low for me. On B003 I am persuaded that the three-person structure (Kane theory, Molenkamp QSH, Xue QAH) is the cleanest of the topological options, cleaner than B018, which leaves out Mele and Hasan. My disagreement is that I would not make it first: it lies in a part of condensed matter where I defer to you and Olle, and the 2016 prize on topological phases is a nearer neighbour than you suggest. I keep it as my second alternative rather than my preferred choice.

responses.point: Topological insulators opened a new class of quantum matter defined by band topology, mature and arguably overdue, with theory and experiment reinforcing each other and agreeing with first-principles calculations.
responses.response: That is a fair and, I think, correct description of the scientific maturity. I would qualify only that QSH, 3D topological insulators and QAH are three discoveries with different heroes, and the compound label B003 leaves Mele, Hasan, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang outside, so a citation should be written narrowly. If the committee prefers condensed matter this year I could support B003 as a fall-back configuration.

responses.point: IceCube opened a new window on the universe through the diffuse neutrino flux and the TXS 0506+056 association, which he values as a discovery made by nature, and he ranks it first.
responses.response: I defer to you on astroparticle physics and agree that the diffuse flux is established and important. My reservation is attribution rather than science: AMANDA, Baikal and the very large collaboration make a Halzen and Karle pair hard to defend as the whole story, and I would like you to say who you think should be left out and why. I rank it last of my list for these reasons, not because I doubt the discovery.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept lattice clocks as a new physical regime rather than a precision refinement of earlier frequency-comb and ion-clock prizes.
Whether leaving out Lemonde, Takamoto and the ion-clock groups is acceptable with a Katori and Ye pair.
How much the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize should reduce the chance for circuit QED (B039), and how the theory share among Blais, Huang and Girvin is to be resolved.
The effect of a possible redefinition of the SI second on the timing of a clock prize.
statement.conflict_note: Potential conflict: I am Director of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and a long-time colleague of Chalmers superconducting-circuit groups, and I have professional links to the circuit QED community (B039), including Schoelkopf, Wallraff and Blais. I ranked B039 first in my opening ballot and therefore should not argue for it as the preferred choice, and I would consider recusing myself on it. No specific personal or institutional connection to the clock candidate B015 (Katori, Ye) is apparent from my profile.
